text: The molar conductivity of a solution of a weak acid HX (0.01 M) is 10 times smaller than the molar conductivity of a solution of a weak acid HY (0.10 M). If λx° ≈ λy°, the difference in their pKa values, pKa(HX) - pKa(HY), is (consider degree of ionization of both acids to be << 1)

design.system: Aqueous solutions of two weak monoprotic acids, HX (0.01 M) and HY (0.10 M), at the same temperature with negligible degree of ionization.
design.hidden_link: The degree of dissociation α links molar conductivity (Λm / Λ°m) to the acid dissociation constant Ka (via Ostwald's dilution law Ka ≈ Cα²).
design.route: Formula 1 (α = Λm/Λ°m): takes the ratio of molar conductivities and equal limiting molar conductivities to give the ratio of degrees of dissociation α(HX)/α(HY) = 1/10. design.trap: Directly using Λm without squaring α when setting up the Ka expression, or forgetting to invert the sign when converting Ka ratio to pKa difference.
design.given: concentrations of both weak acids, ratio of their molar conductivities, condition that limiting molar conductivities are approximately equal, condition that degree of ionization is much less than 1
design.hidden: absolute values of molar conductivities, limiting molar conductivities, and individual Ka values
design.asked: difference in pKa values, pKa(HX) - pKa(HY), dimensionless
design.why_hard: It combines electrochemistry (Arrhenius/Kohlrausch relation for α) with ionic equilibrium (Ostwald's dilution law) purely through proportional reasoning without providing absolute conductivity values.

text: The diffusion coefficient of an ideal gas is proportional to its mean free path and mean speed. The absolute temperature of an ideal gas is increased 4 times and its pressure is increased 2 times. As a result, the diffusion coefficient of this gas increases x times. The value of x is
note: D ∝ λ·ū: factor when T ×4 and P ×2

design.system: An ideal gas undergoing changes in absolute temperature and pressure.
design.hidden_link: Temperature ($T$) and pressure ($P$) simultaneously control both the mean free path ($\lambda \propto T/P$) and mean speed ($\bar{u} \propto \sqrt{T}$), which multiply to determine the diffusion coefficient ($D$).
design.route: Formula 1: takes temperature and pressure factors to find the scaling factor of mean free path ($\lambda \propto T/P$). Formula 2: takes temperature factor to find the scaling factor of mean speed ($\bar{u} \propto \sqrt{T}$), then multiplies them to give the scaling factor of the diffusion coefficient ($D \propto T^{3/2}/P$).
design.student_must_notice: The mean free path $\lambda$ is directly proportional to temperature and inversely proportional to pressure, while average speed $\bar{u}$ depends solely on $\sqrt{T}$.
design.trap: Assuming mean free path depends only on pressure (forgetting the $T$ dependence in $\lambda = k_B T / (\sqrt{2}\pi d^2 P)$) or misidentifying how mean speed scales with temperature.
design.given: proportionality relation between diffusion coefficient, mean free path, and mean speed; factor of increase in absolute temperature; factor of increase in pressure
design.hidden: explicit dependence of mean free path on temperature and pressure, explicit dependence of mean speed on temperature
design.asked: the factor $x$ by which the diffusion coefficient increases, dimensionless
design.why_hard: Students often recall that $\lambda$ is inversely proportional to pressure but forget its direct proportionality to temperature at constant pressure.

text: Consider an electrochemical cell: A(s) | An+(aq, 2M) || B2n+(aq, 1M) | B(s). The value of ΔH° for the cell reaction is twice that of ΔG° at 300 K. design.system: Electrochemical cell 2A(s) + B2n+(aq, 1 M) -> 2An+(aq, 2 M) + B(s) at 300 K.
design.hidden_link: The reaction quotient Q relates cell potential to standard potential via the Nernst equation, connecting E° directly to ΔG° via ΔG° = -nFE°.
design.route: Nernst equation: takes concentrations and E = 0 to give E° (or directly gives ΔG° via RT ln Q); Gibbs-Helmholtz relation: takes ΔH° = 2ΔG° and T = 300 K to give ΔS° = -ΔG°/T.
design.student_must_notice: Balancing the cell reaction per mole of B formed requires 2 moles of An+, so Q = [An+]^2 / [B2n+] = 2^2 / 1 = 4 with 2n electrons transferred, yielding ΔG° = RT ln Q = 2n F E°.
design.trap: Forgetting to square [An+] when writing the reaction quotient Q, or miscounting the number of electrons transferred per mole of B formed.
design.given: Cell notation with concentrations, ratio of standard enthalpy to standard Gibbs free energy, cell emf at 300 K, temperature, gas constant, and natural logarithm of 2
design.hidden: The balanced redox stoichiometry, the reaction quotient Q, the standard cell potential E°, and standard Gibbs free energy change ΔG°
design.asked: ΔS° of the cell reaction per mole of B formed at 300 K, in J K−1 mol−1
design.why_hard: It combines Nernst equation stoichiometry with thermodynamic relations (ΔG° = ΔH° - TΔS°) while requiring careful attention to the stoichiometric coefficient of An+ in Q.

text: Consider a 70% efficient hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell working under standard conditions at 1 bar and 298 K. Its cell reaction is H2(g) + ½O2(g) → H2O(l). design.route: Formula 1 takes the standard electrode potentials of cathode and anode to give E°cell. Formula 2 takes E°cell and n = 2 to give ΔG°. Formula 3 takes ΔG°, the moles of H2 consumed, and the 70% efficiency to give the actual useful work done on the gas. design.student_must_notice: The cell reaction H2(g) + 1/2 O2(g) -> H2O(l) involves a 2-electron transfer (n = 2), and for an adiabatic process in an insulated container, the compression work translates entirely to an increase in internal energy via ΔU = nCvΔT with Cv = 1.5R.
design.trap: Using n = 1 instead of n = 2 for the fuel cell reaction, or forgetting to multiply by the 70% efficiency factor.
design.given: efficiency of fuel cell, temperature and pressure of the cell, moles of H2 consumed, moles and atomicity of ideal gas, reduction potentials of O2/H2O and H+/H2, Faraday's constant, universal gas constant
design.hidden: number of electrons transferred in the cell reaction (n = 2), molar heat capacity at constant volume of a monoatomic ideal gas (Cv = 3/2 R)
design.asked: change in the temperature of the ideal gas, in K
design.why_hard: It bridges electrochemistry and thermodynamics by linking fuel-cell electrical work through an efficiency factor to the adiabatic heating of an ideal gas.

text: At 298 K the limiting molar conductivity of a weak monobasic acid is 4×10² S cm² mol⁻¹. At 298 K for an aqueous solution of the acid the degree of dissociation is α and the molar conductivity is y×10² S cm² mol⁻¹. design.hidden_link: The acid dissociation constant (K_a) remains invariant before and after dilution, linking the two states via Ostwald's dilution law.
design.route: Formula 1 gives initial α = y/4 and diluted α' = 3y/4 = 3α. Formula 2 equates K_a for both states: Cα²/(1 - α) = (C/20)(3α)²/(1 - 3α) to solve directly for α.
design.student_must_notice: Since molar conductivity triples upon dilution, the new degree of dissociation is exactly 3α, allowing K_a equality without needing absolute values of C or y.
design.trap: Using the approximation 1 - α ≈ 1, which leads to an inconsistent contradiction (1 = 9/20) and fails to determine α.
design.given: Limiting molar conductivity of the weak acid, molar conductivity at initial concentration in terms of y, factor of dilution (20 times), and new molar conductivity in terms of y.

design.asked: Degree of dissociation (α) of the initial solution, dimensionless
design.why_hard: Solvers cannot use the standard weak-electrolyte approximation (1 - α ≈ 1) and must equate the full Ostwald dilution law expressions to cancel out the unknown concentration.

text: To form a complete monolayer of acetic acid on 1g of charcoal, 100 mL of 0.5 M acetic acid was used. Some of the acetic acid remained unadsorbed. To neutralize the unadsorbed acetic acid, 40 mL of 1 M NaOH solution was required. If each molecule of acetic acid occupies P × 10⁻²³ m² surface area on charcoal, the value of P is [Use: Surface area of charcoal = 1.5×10² m² g⁻¹; Avogadro's number (N_A) = 6.0×10²³ mol⁻¹]
note: acid taken − acid left (back titration) -> molecules adsorbed -> area each

design.system: Acetic acid monolayer adsorption on charcoal surface from aqueous solution, with remaining unadsorbed acid neutralized by aqueous NaOH.
design.hidden_link: The moles of acetic acid actually adsorbed on the charcoal surface bridges the solution-phase back-titration stoichiometry with the surface area calculation.
design.route: Formula 1: takes initial moles of acetic acid and moles of NaOH used to neutralize unadsorbed acid, gives moles (and then total number of molecules) of adsorbed acetic acid. Formula 2: takes total surface area of charcoal and total adsorbed molecules, gives cross-sectional surface area per molecule (and thus the coefficient P).
design.student_must_notice: The amount of acetic acid forming the monolayer is the difference between the total initial acid and the unadsorbed acid determined by neutralization with NaOH.
design.trap: Directly using the initial amount of acetic acid to calculate the number of adsorbed molecules without subtracting the unadsorbed fraction.
design.given: mass of charcoal, volume and molarity of initial acetic acid, volume and molarity of NaOH required for neutralization, specific surface area of charcoal, Avogadro's constant
design.hidden: moles of unadsorbed acetic acid, moles of adsorbed acetic acid, total number of adsorbed molecules
design.asked: value of P (where area per molecule = P × 10⁻²³ m²), dimensionless
design.why_hard: It combines volumetric back-titration concepts with surface chemistry (monolayer coverage and cross-sectional area per molecule).
